questions.question: If two cars travel the same distance, but Car A has a greater speed than Car B, how will their travel times compare?
options: Car A takes a shorter time than Car B.
Car A takes a longer time than Car B.
Both cars take the exact same time.
Car A takes twice as much time as Car B.

questions.question: Which formula is used to calculate the speed of an object?
options: Speed = distance + time
Speed = distance × time
Speed = distance ÷ time
Speed = time ÷ distance

questions.question: What does the speed unit 'm/s' (metres per second) specifically represent?
options: The total distance divided by the total mass of the object.
The number of metres travelled each second.
The acceleration of an object in one minute.
The force required to move one metre.

questions.question: On a distance-time graph, how can you tell if an object is moving at a faster speed?
options: The line is perfectly horizontal.
The line has a steeper gradient.
The line curves downwards to the time axis.
The line is closer to the bottom edge of the graph.

questions.question: When does a falling object reach its terminal velocity?
options: When the gravitational force is twice as large as the drag force.
When the drag force and the gravitational force are equal.
When there is no gravity acting on the object at all.
When the drag force becomes zero.

questions.question: Why does a larger parachute help a skydiver slow down more?
options: The larger surface area creates a bigger drag force.
The larger surface area decreases the gravitational force.
The larger surface area increases the weight of the skydiver.
The larger surface area eliminates air resistance completely.

questions.question: What does a flat, level horizontal line represent on a distance-time graph?
options: The object is moving at a constant high speed.
The object is accelerating rapidly.
The object is stationary and not moving.
The object is returning to its starting point.

questions.question: On a distance-time graph, what do upward and downward sloping lines represent?
options: Movement in opposite directions.
Movement at the exact same constant speed.
The object is speeding up in both cases.
The object has stopped moving entirely.

questions.question: What is meant by the 'instantaneous speed' of an object?
options: The total distance travelled divided by the total journey time.
The average speed calculated over a whole day.
The speed of the object at a particular moment in time.
The speed of an object when it is at rest.

questions.question: Why do scientists take repeat readings during an experiment?
options: To make the experiment take longer to complete.
To reduce the effect of random errors.
To guarantee that no anomalous data can occur.
To change the independent variable of the test.

questions.question: If you identify an anomalous reading in your scientific data, what should you do with it?
options: Include it in the calculation of your average to be fair.
Multiply it by two to balance the other results.
Do not use it in your calculations of averages.
Replace all other successful trials with this reading.

questions.question: In which direction does the force of friction always act?
options: In the same direction as the movement of the object.
Downwards towards the centre of the Earth.
Against the direction of movement of the object.
Upwards, perpendicular to the surface.

questions.question: What will happen to an object moving at a steady speed in a straight line if no resultant force acts on it?
options: It will gradually slow down and stop.
It will continue to move at a steady speed in a straight line.
It will instantly change its direction.
It will speed up indefinitely.

questions.question: What is the primary physical effect of streamlining a vehicle?
options: It increases the gravitational pull on the vehicle.
It reduces the drag force acting on the vehicle.
It increases the friction between the tyres and the road.
It makes the vehicle heavier and more stable.

questions.question: How does the drag force on an object moving through a fluid change as its speed increases?
options: The drag force increases with speed.
The drag force decreases to zero.
The drag force remains completely constant.
The drag force changes direction randomly.

questions.question: What effect can a resultant force have on the speed of an object?
options: It has no effect on the speed under any circumstances.
It can change the speed of the object.
It only keeps the speed exactly constant.
It can only decrease the speed, never increase it.

questions.question: Which of the following describes how gravity pulls down on a falling object?
options: With a force that increases every second.
With a steady force.
With a force that decreases as speed increases.
With a force that depends on the shape of the object.

questions.question: When timing a race with a stopwatch, how should your eyes be positioned to help you stop the watch at the right moment?
options: High above the track looking down at an angle.
In line with the finish line.
Looking directly at the buttons on the stopwatch.
Focused on the starting blocks.

questions.question: What does a single point on a distance-time graph directly describe?
options: The instantaneous speed of the object.
The average speed of the entire journey.
Where the object is at a specific point in time.
The total acceleration of the object.

questions.question: How does streamlining help an object move through a fluid more easily?
options: It reduces how much fluid needs to be pushed out of the way.
It increases the density of the fluid surrounding the object.
It allows gravity to pull the object forward instead of down.
It creates a vacuum directly in front of the moving object.
